summary: Extends the Link Management Protocol with a way to negotiate capabilities and indicate support for LMP extensions. It is compatible with implementations that do not support it, and it updates several earlier LMP and GMPLS RFCs.

plainLanguage.summary: Two machines swap short lists of what each knows how to do, so they use only the features both understand.

questions: what is the lmp behaviorconfig object
how do lmp nodes discover supported extensions
subtitle: A generic capability flag in LMP Config messages lets neighbors discover which LMP extensions each supports.

tldr.problem: The Link Management Protocol had no generic way for a node to learn which LMP extensions its neighbor supports, so the right features could not be selected safely.
tldr.mechanism: A new BehaviorConfig CONFIG object (C-Type 3) carries flag bits for the Trace, DWDM and data channel consistency check behaviors, and Config, ConfigAck and ConfigNack messages may now carry multiple CONFIG objects.
tldr.outcome: Nodes can discover each other's supported behaviors and fall back to older Config usage when a neighbor does not support the extension. It updates RFC 4204, RFC 4207, RFC 4209 and RFC 5818.

today: RFC 6898 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2013 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It updates RFC 4204, RFC 4207, RFC 4209 and RFC 5818.

sections.title: Why LMP Needs Behavior Negotiation
sections.content:
The Link Management Protocol (LMP, RFC 4204) is used in networks controlled by GMPLS. Extensions have since been added: the Trace behavior for SONET/SDH (RFC 4207, message types 21 to 31), DWDM support (RFC 4209) and the data channel consistency check (RFC 5818, message types 32 to 34).

If one node supports a new behavior and its neighbor does not, a mechanism is needed to discover peer capabilities. The base specification has none, and RFC 4209 defined one only for its own functions. This RFC defines a generic one and says how a supporting node deals with legacy nodes.
sections.plainLanguage: Machines got new skills over time, but had no way to ask each other which skills they have. This adds a way to ask.

sections.title: Multiple CONFIG Objects in Messages
sections.content:
The Config and ConfigNack messages used to carry exactly one CONFIG object, and ConfigAck carried none. This RFC lets all three carry one or more, using Backus-Naur Form from RFC 5511. ConfigAck now echoes CONFIG objects so negotiated parameters are explicit.

At most one object of any C-Type SHALL be included. A receiver processes the first object of a C-Type and ignores later ones of the same type. Order of objects with different C-Types is not significant unless their definition says so.
sections.plainLanguage: Before, each note could hold one card. Now a note can hold several different cards, but never two of the same kind.

sections.title: The BehaviorConfig Object
sections.content:
The CONFIG object is class 6. Two C-Types existed: 1 for HelloConfig and 2 for LMP-WDM_CONFIG. This RFC adds C-Type 3, BehaviorConfig, whose use signals support for these extensions.

The object holds a flags field with three defined bits: S for the SONET/SDH Trace behavior, D for DWDM behavior and C for the data channel consistency check. The remaining bits are Must Be Zero (MBZ), sized to keep the object 32-bit aligned. Future documents may define more bits.
sections.plainLanguage: The card has three tick boxes: one for each extra skill. All the other boxes must stay empty.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving Behavior Flags
sections.content:
A supporting node MUST include a BehaviorConfig object in a Config message to a neighbor whose support is known or unknown, and MUST NOT send it to a neighbor known not to support it. The N-bit (negotiable) in the object header MUST be set.

In Config and ConfigNack the flags SHOULD reflect the sender's capabilities. In a ConfigAck the flags MUST equal those received, and the ConfigAck MUST include all CONFIG objects from the Config message when it contained a BehaviorConfig. A ConfigNack MUST NOT include acceptable CONFIG objects and MUST include unacceptable ones. A receiver compares the flags with its capacities, and any bit set in the MBZ portion MUST be treated as unacceptable.
sections.plainLanguage: You show your card to a new neighbor unless you know they cannot read it. They copy it back if they agree, or point out what they cannot do.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
A node that does not support the extension may react in four ways: (a) send a ConfigNack for the unknown C-Type, (b) send a ConfigNack for multiple CONFIG objects, (c) silently ignore the objects and reply with a ConfigAck without CONFIG objects, or (d) treat the message as malformed and discard it.

In cases (a) to (c) the sender SHOULD explicitly record that the neighbor lacks support. In case (d) there is no response, and when the retry limit from RFC 4204 is reached the node SHOULD infer lack of support. Once a neighbor is identified as non-supporting, the node SHOULD follow previously defined Config usage.
sections.plainLanguage: An old machine might say it does not understand, ignore the card, or say nothing. In every case the newer machine works out that it should stick to the old ways.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The security measures in RFC 4204 apply equally to the new object, and their use is RECOMMENDED. The procedures alone cause no change in network state, but intercepted or spoofed messages could cause bogus management plane alerts or make peers wrongly believe extensions can or cannot be used. The references have been updated to RFC 4301 and RFC 5996 for IKEv2.

IANA assigned C-Type 3 (BehaviorConfig) in the CONFIG class and created the registry "LMP Behavior Configuration Flags", with allocation by Standards Action. Bit 0 is S, bit 1 is D and bit 2 is C.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone could fake a card and trick the machines about what they can do, so keep the messages protected. A public list records what each tick box means.

fields.name: S
fields.desc: Support for the SONET/SDH Trace behavior.

fields.name: C
fields.desc: Support for the data channel consistency check.

fields.name: Must Be Zero (MBZ)
fields.desc: Remaining bits, set to zero; sized for 32-bit alignment.
